Gut microbiota is implicated in the development and progression of metabolic diseases such as type 2 diabetes, obesity, and non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, though most of the evidence is from mice. These microorganisms reside in the gastrointestinal tract, where they help break down dietary components, synthesize essential nutrients, and regulate the immune system. Turnbaugh's 2006 transplant experiments, which made obese mice from lean ones, started the field. Dysbiosis, an imbalance in the gut microbiota, can lead to chronic inflammation, altered metabolism, and increased insulin resistance, and that is the proposed route to metabolic disease pathogenesis. Diet moves microbial composition and function within days, as David and colleagues showed in 2014, and lifestyle, antibiotics and other environmental factors move it too. Research suggests manipulating the gut microbiota through probiotics, prebiotics and fecal microbiota transplantation as a therapeutic approach. A balanced diet rich in fiber and fewer processed foods remain the reliable advice for a healthy gut microbiome. Personalized medicine strategies that consider individual gut microbiota profiles could make prevention and treatment of metabolic diseases more effective, on the same mouse-heavy evidence.

In this study, we investigated the role of the solvent cavity in substrate binding to OleP by performing mutations at specific positions within this region. The mutations were introduced at two distinct sites: the BC loop at residue E89 and the I helix at residue S240, with the residue G92 located on the BC loop. The mutants were designed based on the previously reported structure of the closed aglycone-bound OleP, with the objective of reducing the volume of the cavity while still allowing the hydrophobic side chains of the mutated residues to fit. This goal was achieved by substituting E89 with tyrosine, G92 with tryptophan, and S240 with tyrosine. To assess the impact of these mutations, we conducted equilibrium binding experiments and analyzed the structural organization of the active site using X-ray crystallography and molecular dynamics (MD) simulations. The substrate analog 6-deoxyerythronolide B (6DEB) was used as the binding substrate. We examined how the introduced mutations affected the aglycone binding properties, the structural organization of the active site, and the conformational plasticity of the OleP-6DEB complex.
